extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in music censorship, media policy, and the history of the Parents Music Resource Center (PMRC)
extracted.subtask_description: Historical account and policy proposals about labeling and restricting music considered explicit; documents the PMRC's recommendations (labels, warnings, retail and broadcast restrictions), the Parental Advisory sticker, and arguments for and against such measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental control over children's access
rubrics_metrics.description: Stated goal of increasing parental control over children's access to music deemed to have violent, drug-related, or sexual themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the PMRC's overarching objective that motivated proposals such as labeling and retail/broadcast restrictions; measures are framed as informing parents and limiting minors' exposure rather than criminalizing artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop music labeling similar to the film rating system
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested a voluntary move by the RIAA and the music industry to develop music labeling in the form of a rating system similar to the film rating system developed by the Motion Picture Association of America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMRC originally proposed a descriptive rating system (categorizing specific types of explicit content) analogous to MPAA film ratings; industry ultimately adopted a more generic advisory label. Guidance/choice point: descriptive vs generic labeling affects informativeness and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print warnings and lyrics on album covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Printing warnings and lyrics on album covers to inform consumers about explicit content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMRC recommended lyrics and warning text be printed on album packaging. In practice the industry implemented 'Parental Advisory' labels and sometimes printed lyrics; proponents argued transparency for parents, opponents warned of misinterpretation and chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retail placement restrictions for explicit albums
rubrics_metrics.description: Require record stores to put albums with explicit covers under the counters or otherwise restrict their display/sale to adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMRC suggested stores place explicit albums out of general view; in response, some retailers refused to carry labeled albums (e.g., Wal‑Mart) or limited sales to adults. Anti-pattern: blanket removal can amount to de facto censorship and reduce access for adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict broadcast of explicit songs and videos
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure television stations and broadcasters not to air explicit songs or music videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMRC urged broadcasters to avoid airing content considered sexually explicit, violent, or occult. This recommendation raises issues of free-speech limits, subjective interpretation of content, and differing standards across media outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassess musician contracts; create industry standards panel
rubrics_metrics.description: Reassess the contracts of musicians who performed violently or sexually in concert, and create a panel to set industry standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PMRC proposed contractual and self-regulatory mechanisms (a panel) to set and enforce content standards. Guidance/concern: contract-based or panel enforcement can institutionalize subjective moral judgments and raise enforcement/interpretation challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectionable content categories (PTA 'R' symbol / Filthy Fifteen categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories used to identify objectionable recordings: explicit sexual language, violence, profanity, the occult, glorification of drugs and alcohol; PMRC's Filthy Fifteen enumerated categories like sex/masturbation, sex, sex/violence, violence/language, drug and alcohol use, occult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PMRC and allied groups (e.g., National PTA proposal) recommended labeling based on such categories; examples (Filthy Fifteen) show how specific songs were classified. Guidance: categorical labeling requires clear definitions to avoid overbroad or prejudicial application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a generic Parental Advisory label (voluntary industry label)
rubrics_metrics.description: RIAA agreed to put 'Parental Advisory' labels on selected releases at their own discretion; the labels were generic (not descriptive of which content category triggered the label).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic labels were less informative than PMRC's proposed descriptive labels. Effects noted: some stores refused to sell labeled albums or restricted sales to adults; effectiveness in preventing exposure is uncertain and may produce a 'forbidden-fruit' sales boost. Artists and critics argued labels could increase sales or stigmatize work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections: censorship, civil liberties infringement, misinterpretation, and counterproductivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms that labeling proposals amount to censorship, infringe on civil liberties, encourage misinterpretation of art, and may be counterproductive (the 'forbidden-fruit effect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposing witnesses (Frank Zappa, John Denver, Dee Snider) argued labels are 'an ill-conceived piece of nonsense', infringe rights, and risk misinterpreting artists' intent; policymakers should weigh free-speech implications and enforcement/interpretation problems. Historical examples: testimony comparing labeling to Nazi book burnings; concern that suppression increases attraction to content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prejudicial targeting and moral panic against genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of prejudicial targeting of specific music genres (e.g., heavy metal) and moral-panic framing (accusations of Satanic/occult themes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PMRC was criticized for disproportionately focusing on heavy metal and for moral‑panic rhetoric. Guidance: fair, transparent criteria should avoid singling out genres or applying moralistic labels without clear, objective standards.
